claim: GWAS with sample sizes of over one million participants have identified hundreds of genetic variants (single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs) that associate with educational attainment and other social phenotypes.
source: GWAS with sample sizes of over one million participants have identified hundreds of genetic variants (single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs) that associate with educational attainment and other social phenotypes (Lee et al., 2018; Karlsson Linnér et al., 2019; Luciano et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published GWAS studies

claim: Individual SNPs associate only very weakly with complex polygenic phenotypes in isolation, typically accounting for less than 0.01% of variation.
source: While individual SNPs associate only very weakly with complex polygenic phenotypes in isolation - typically accounting for less than 0.01% of variation
evidence: Based on established understanding from genetic studies

claim: In the most recent education GWAS, the median per allele effect size of lead SNPs related to an additional 1.7 weeks of schooling.
source: For example, in the most recent education GWAS, the median per allele effect size of lead SNPs related to an additional 1.7 weeks of schooling
evidence: Reported finding from cited GWAS study

claim: Polygenic scores combining all identified SNPs explained up to 13% of the variance in years of educational attainment in out of sample prediction samples.
source: but polygenic scores combining all identified SNPs explained up to 13% of the variance in years of educational attainment (defined as completed years of education) and 9.2% of the variation in educational achievement (defined as high school grade point average [GPA]) in out of sample prediction samples (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Reported finding from cited GWAS study

claim: Polygenic scores combining all identified SNPs explained 9.2% of the variation in educational achievement (high school GPA) in out of sample prediction samples.
source: but polygenic scores combining all identified SNPs explained up to 13% of the variance in years of educational attainment (defined as completed years of education) and 9.2% of the variation in educational achievement (defined as high school grade point average [GPA]) in out of sample prediction samples (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Reported finding from cited GWAS study

claim: Polygenic scores have been promoted as a potential tool for genetically informed policy.
source: are increasingly being used as indicators of genetic propensity, and have been promoted as a potential tool for genetically informed policy (Plomin, 2018; Conley and Fletcher, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to publications promoting this use

claim: It has been suggested that genetic information could be used prescriptively to provide personalised medicine, education and even dating.
source: It has been suggested that genetic information could be used prescriptively to provide personalised medicine, education and even dating (Plomin, 2018; McCarthy and Mahajan, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to publications suggesting these applications

claim: Personalised learning was adopted in national policy statements in England in 2004 with a focus on the needs of individual students.
source: Personalised learning was adopted in national policy statements in England in 2004 with a focus on the needs of individual students (Gilbert, 2020; Department for Children, Schools and Families, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to policy documents

claim: Personalised learning was not mandated and was seen as being conceptually ambiguous, leading to inconsistency in its implementation across schools.
source: However, it was not mandated and was seen as being conceptually ambiguous, leading to inconsistency in its implementation across schools (Maguire et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on policy implementation

claim: There are currently no policies in place that rely on educational prediction.
source: There are currently no policies in place that rely on educational prediction
evidence: Statement about current policy landscape

claim: Calls are increasingly being made for genetic data to be used to personalise education to identify pupils in need of greater educational support.
source: but calls are increasingly being made for genetic data to be used to personalise education to, for example, identify pupils in need of greater educational support (Miller, 1990; Grigorenko, 2007; Sabatello, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to publications calling for this use

claim: Polygenic scores for education associate with many aspects of environment and schooling.
source: Given the social complexity of educational attainment, polygenic scores for education associate with many aspects of environment and schooling (Abdellaoui et al., 2019; Harden et al., 2020), referred to as gene-environment correlation.
evidence: Supported by citations to research demonstrating these associations

claim: Active gene-environment correlation can be thought of as environment downstream of genotype.
source: Active gene-environment correlation can be thought of as environment downstream of genotype; for example, pupil's selecting certain subjects based on their genotype.
evidence: Conceptual definition with example

claim: Passive gene-environment correlation can be thought of as environment upstream of genotype.
source: Passive gene-environment correlation can be thought of as environment upstream of genotype; for example, children of highly educated parents being more likely to inherit education associated environments as well as education associated genes (Kong et al., 2018) (also referred to as dynastic effects Davies et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: Conceptual definition with example and citations

claim: A person's education polygenic score associates with a range of phenotypic differences very early in life.
source: That a person's education polygenic score associates with a range of phenotypic differences very early in life demonstrates that it captures a very broad range of information, not just their education.
evidence: Inference from observed associations

claim: Polygenic scores are more predictive when genetic factors play a larger role in a phenotype (as measured by heritability).
source: Briefly, polygenic scores are more predictive when genetic factors play a larger role in a phenotype (as measured by heritability), and in the case of binary phenotypes where prevalence in the outcome is higher (Janssens et al., 2006; Wray et al., 2010; Zhao and Zou, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on polygenic score prediction

claim: In the case of binary phenotypes, polygenic scores are more predictive where prevalence in the outcome is higher.
source: Briefly, polygenic scores are more predictive when genetic factors play a larger role in a phenotype (as measured by heritability), and in the case of binary phenotypes where prevalence in the outcome is higher (Janssens et al., 2006; Wray et al., 2010; Zhao and Zou, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on polygenic score prediction

claim: Phenotypic measures such as sex, month of birth and prior achievement are predictive of educational achievement.
source: Phenotypic measures that are predictive of educational achievement such as sex, month of birth and prior achievement (Benton et al., 2004; Solli, 2017) are readily available to schools
evidence: Supported by citations to research demonstrating these associations

claim: Parental education and socioeconomic position are predictive of educational achievement.
source: while other measures such as parental education and socioeconomic position (Morris et al., 2016; Strand, 2011) are, in principle, simple and inexpensive to collect.
evidence: Supported by citations to research demonstrating these associations

claim: Few studies have investigated how well polygenic scores predict individual level educational attainment or achievement conditional on observable phenotypes that are easily available to educators.
source: To date, few studies have investigated how well polygenic scores predict individual level educational attainment or achievement conditional on observable phenotypes that are easily available to educators.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature

claim: Children with higher polygenic scores, on average, had higher exam scores than those with lower polygenic scores.
source: Children with higher polygenic scores, on average, had higher exam scores than those with lower polygenic scores.
evidence: Inference from correlation data

claim: Correlations between predictors and achievement were consistently stronger for age 16 than age 7 educational achievement.
source: Correlations were consistently stronger for age 16 than age 7 educational achievement.
evidence: Comparison of correlation coefficients from study data

claim: Both the genomewide significant and the all SNP polygenic scores accounted for a larger proportion of variance explained (R2) in achievement than age and sex alone.
source: Both the genomewide significant and the all SNP polygenic scores accounted for a larger proportion of variance explained (R2) in achievement than age and sex alone.
evidence: Comparison of R2 values from regression analyses

claim: Pupil characteristics outperformed polygenic scores in terms of explanatory power for age 7 achievement.
source: Pupil characteristics outperformed polygenic scores in terms of explanatory power
evidence: Comparison of R2 values from regression analyses shown in Figure 1

claim: Polygenic scores and pupil characteristics together explained up to 21.5% (95% CI: 18.9 to 24.1) of the variation in age 7 achievement.
source: but together they explained up to 21.5% (95% CI: 18.9 to 24.1) of the variation in age 7 achievement.
evidence: R2 value with confidence interval from regression analysis

claim: Including information on the social background of pupils' parents that is potentially obtainable by schools further increased the explanatory power of the models up to a maximum R2 of 26.3% (23.4 to 29.2) for age 7 achievement.
source: Including information on the social background of pupils' parents that is potentially obtainable by schools further increased the explanatory power of the models up to a maximum R2 of 26.3% (23.4 to 29.2).
evidence: R2 value with confidence interval from regression analysis

claim: The incremental R2 of the polygenic scores over pupil characteristics were 1.8% (-0.7 to 4.3) and 4.8 (2.1 to 7.3) for age 7 achievement.
source: The incremental R2 of the polygenic scores over pupil characteristics were 1.8% (-0.7 to 4.3) and 4.8 (2.1 to 7.3), suggesting that they provide some additional predictive information over currently available or easily collectable data.
evidence: Incremental R2 values with confidence intervals from regression analyses

claim: The genomewide significant and all SNP polygenic scores explained an additional 3.4% (1.7 to 5.0) and 12.9% (10.6 to 15.3) of educational achievement at age 16 over age and sex alone.
source: The genomewide significant and all SNP polygenic scores explained more variation of achievement in exams sat at the end of compulsory education at age 16, explaining an additional 3.4% (1.7 to 5.0) and 12.9% (10.6 to 15.3) of educational achievement over age and sex alone (Figure 2B).
evidence: Incremental R2 values with confidence intervals from regression analyses shown in Figure 2B

claim: Measures of parental education and socioeconomic position provided greater returns to explanatory power than the polygenic scores when unadjusted for prior achievement, explaining an additional 19% (16.6 to 21.4) and 21.4% (18.8 to 23.9) respectively over age and sex for age 16 achievement.
source: By comparison, measures of parental education and socioeconomic position provided greater returns to explanatory power than the polygenic scores when unadjusted for prior achievement, explaining an additional 19% (16.6 to 21.4) and 21.4% (18.8 to 23.9) respectively over age and sex (Figure 2B).
evidence: Incremental R2 values with confidence intervals from regression analyses shown in Figure 2B

claim: Prior achievement at age 14 explained 65.1% (60.9 to 69.4) of the variation in age 16 achievement alongside age and sex.
source: For example, prior achievement at age 14 explained 65.1% (60.9 to 69.4) of the variation in age 16 achievement alongside age and sex (Figure 2A).
evidence: R2 value with confidence interval from regression analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Conditional on prior achievement data, the polygenic scores provide very little discernible increase in explanatory power for age 16 achievement.
source: Conditional on prior achievement data, the polygenic scores provide very little discernible increase in explanatory power (Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparison of incremental R2 values shown in Figure 2B

claim: There is near complete overlap in the distributions of polygenic scores between high achieving pupils at age 16 and all other pupils.
source: The polygenic scores of high achievers are, on average, higher than of other pupils, but there is near complete overlap in the distributions between the groups.
evidence: Visual inspection of distributions shown in Figure 3

claim: The near complete overlap in polygenic score distributions suggests there would be a large proportion of misclassification when trying to predict from genetic data whether a pupil will be in the top 10%.
source: This suggests there would be a large proportion of misclassification when trying to predict from genetic data whether a pupil will be in the top 10%.
evidence: Inference from observed distribution overlap

claim: There is far less overlap in the distributions of prior achievement between high achievers and other pupils compared to polygenic scores.
source: By comparison, there is far less overlap in the distributions of prior achievement between high achievers and other pupils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Visual comparison of distributions shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: While some pupils are correctly predicted from their genetic data to be high achievers, a greater proportion are erroneously predicted to be in the wrong group.
source: Figure 4 displays this misclassification of pupils; while some are correctly predicted from their genetic data to be high achievers, a greater proportion are erroneously predicted to be in the wrong group.
evidence: Visual display of misclassification shown in Figure 4

claim: Misclassification from polygenic scores is similar for parental education and socioeconomic position but lower for prior attainment.
source: This misclassification is similar for parental education and socioeconomic position but lower for prior attainment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of misclassification patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The group of pupils predicted to be in the top 10% of achievers will on average perform higher than other pupils in exams, but the large variability shows that many of the pupils in this group will not ultimately be in the top 10%.
source: In each case, the group of pupils predicted to be in the top 10% of achievers will on average perform higher than other pupils in exams, but the large variability shows that many of the pupils in this group will not ultimately be in the top 10%.
evidence: Inference from observed variability in predictions

claim: Compared to measures of parental socioeconomic position (AUCs: 0.70 for both years of education and social class), the polygenic scores have a lower AUC and therefore poorer sensitivity and specificity to discriminate high achievers at age 7 (AUCs: 0.63 for the GWAS sig PGS; 0.68 for the All SNP PGS).
source: Compared to measures of parental socioeconomic position (AUCs: 0.70 for both years of education and social class), the polygenic scores have a lower AUC and therefore poorer sensitivity and specificity to discriminate high achievers at age 7 (AUCs: 0.63 for the GWAS sig PGS; 0.68 for the All SNP PGS) (Figure 5).

claim: The trade-off in sensitivity and specificity for each of the measures at different classification thresholds is poor; high sensitivity comes at the cost of low specificity (and vice versa).
source: The trade-off in sensitivity and specificity for each of the measures at different classification thresholds is also poor; high sensitivity comes at the cost of low specificity (and vice versa).
evidence: Interpretation of ROC curves shown in Figure 5

claim: In order to accurately identify most of the pupils who will go on to be in the top 10% of achievers, one would have to set the classification at the point where almost all students would be identified.
source: This means that in order to accurately identify most of the pupils who will go on to be in the top 10% of achievers, one would have to set the classification at the point where almost all students would be identified.
evidence: Inference from ROC curve analysis

claim: The results were consistent when other cut-offs were used to determine the high achieving group, suggesting that the results do not reflect the definition of high achievers.
source: These results were consistent when other cut-offs were used to determine the high achieving group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the results do not reflect our definition of high achievers.
evidence: Sensitivity analysis using different cut-offs shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: At age 16, measures of prior achievement provide far higher sensitivity and specificity for predicting educational achievement than the polygenic scores (AUCs: 0.83 to 0.95 for prior achievement compared to 0.61 to 0.70 for the polygenic scores).
source: Figure 6a shows that measures of prior achievement provide far higher sensitivity and specificity for predicting educational achievement than the polygenic scores (AUCs: 0.83 to 0.95 for prior achievement compared to 0.61 to 0.70 for the polygenic scores).

claim: A classification point can be set for prior achievement at age 14 with a sensitivity and specificity of around 0.85, whereas the best classification point for polygenic scores would give a sensitivity and specificity of around 0.65.
source: For example, a classification point can be set for prior achievement at age 14 with a sensitivity and specificity of around 0.85, whereas the best classification point for polygenic scores would give a sensitivity and specificity of around 0.65.

source: As with achievement at age 7, the ROC curve for the All SNP polygenic score was similar to the ROC curves for parent's years of education and socioeconomic position (Figure 6b).

claim: After accounting for the phenotypic information already available to schools, the polygenic scores provide almost no information to reliably identify high achievers (AUC: 0.51 and 0.56).
source: The results (Figure 6c) demonstrated that after accounting for the phenotypic information already available to schools, the polygenic scores provide almost no information to reliably identify high achievers (AUC: 0.51 and 0.56).

source: The results were consistent had these predictions been made earlier in schooling where later measures of prior attainment were unavailable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; AUC's: 0.54 to 0.61).

source: If they selected the students with the top 10% of polygenic scores, they would on average only sample 24% of the top 10% highest achievers at age 16, and 76% of those not in the top 10%.

claim: If the principal or policy maker used phenotypic measures from age 11, they would sample 51% of the top 10% highest achievers at age 16, and 49% of those not in the top 10%.
source: In contrast, if the principal or policy maker used phenotypic measures from age 11, they would sample 51% of the top 10% highest achievers at age 16, and 49% of those not in the top 10%.

claim: Polygenic scores cannot be used to identify high achieving students more accurately than available phenotypic measures.
source: This suggests that polygenic scores cannot be used to identify high achieving students more accurately than available phenotypic measures.
evidence: Inference from classification accuracy comparisons

claim: The group of pupils with the highest polygenic scores do - on average - have higher achievement, but the predictive information provided from the polygenic scores is inferior to that provided by phenotypic predictors.
source: The group of pupils with the highest polygenic scores do - on average - have higher achievement, but the predictive information provided from the polygenic scores is inferior to that provided by phenotypic predictors.

claim: The polygenic scores were predictive of educational achievement, accounting for 3.4% and 12.9% of the variance (above age and sex) across the sample at age 7 and 16 respectively.
source: Our results demonstrated that the polygenic scores were predictive of educational achievement, accounting for 3.4% and 12.9% of the variance (above age and sex) across our sample at age 7 and 16 respectively.

claim: For informative education predictions at the individual level, the most predictive measure was prior achievement.
source: For informative education predictions at the individual level, the most predictive measure was prior achievement.

source: Genetic data from individuals therefore provided little information on their future achievement over phenotypic data that is either available or easily obtainable by educators.

source: This is consistent with results from the only other study we are aware of to assess incremental variance explained over parental social characteristics, which observed higher variance explained in years of education by parental education (18% to 21.3%) than the polygenic score (10.6% to 12.7%) in two US samples (Lee et al., 2018).

source: The lack of genotypic predictive power that we observed over and above phenotypic data may be because prior achievement mediates genotypic effects on educational outcomes; genetic variants that affect educational achievement at earlier ages are likely to also affect achievement at later ages.

source: genetic variants that affect educational achievement at earlier ages are likely to also affect achievement at later ages.

evidence: Inference from heritability with citation to theoretical work

claim: Issues from confounding biases caused by population level phenomena such as population stratification, assortative mating and dynastic effects (genetic nurture) may have impacted the results.
source: Finally, issues from confounding biases caused by population level phenomena such as population stratification, assortative mating and dynastic effects (genetic nurture) (Kong et al., 2018; Morris et al., 2019; Bates et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018) may have impacted our results.
evidence: Statement about potential biases with citations

claim: Confounding biases can lead to social and family differences being masked as genetic differences between individuals, inflating associations between polygenic scores and educational achievement in between individual analyses.
source: These biases can lead to social and family differences being masked as genetic differences between individuals, inflating associations between polygenic scores and educational achievement in between individual analyses.
evidence: Explanation of how biases affect results

claim: Family data are required to further investigate the impact of confounding biases.
source: Family data are required to further investigate the impact of these baises (Brumpton et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited methodological requirement for addressing biases

claim: Currently available genetic scores are unlikely to provide more accurate predictions of how well a pupil will perform in school exams than easily measured phenotypes.
source: In conclusion, our results suggest that currently available genetic scores are unlikely to provide more accurate predictions of how well a pupil will perform in school exams than easily measured phenotypes.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all analyses

claim: Genetic data provide little additional information on an individual's school performance over and above more readily available and easily collected phenotypic data, except where prior achievement measures are unavailable.
source: Genetic data provide little additional information on an individual's school performance over and above more readily available and easily collected phenotypic data, except where prior achievement measures are unavailable.
evidence: Summary conclusion from incremental prediction analyses

claim: The greatest value of genetic data may lie for researchers investigating the etiology of educational differences between groups of pupils, teachers and schools.
source: The greatest value of genetic data may lie instead for researchers investigating the etiology of educational differences between groups of pupils, teachers and schools and for novel sociogenomic analyses into socioeconomic inequalities in education achievement and attainment.
evidence: Inference about appropriate applications of genetic data

claim: Genetic data may be valuable for novel sociogenomic analyses into socioeconomic inequalities in education achievement and attainment.
source: The greatest value of genetic data may lie instead for researchers investigating the etiology of educational differences between groups of pupils, teachers and schools and for novel sociogenomic analyses into socioeconomic inequalities in education achievement and attainment.

claim: The study used average fine graded point scores at four major Key Stages of education in the UK: Key Stage 1 (age 7), Key Stage 2 (age 11), Key Stage 3 (age 14), and Key Stage 4 (age 16).
